claims.text: High-entropy alloys can undergo thermally induced toughness or ductility loss at temperatures above 500°C.
Adding less than 1 wt% boron to a high-entropy alloy will improve its resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
The proposed effect applies to high-entropy alloys in either an as-cast or wrought initial state.
The proposed effect should occur after extended exposure above 500°C followed by cooling to room temperature.
Boron atoms will segregate to grain boundaries in the treated high-entropy alloy.
Grain-boundary segregation of boron will reduce grain-boundary energy.
Grain-boundary segregation of boron will enhance cohesion between grains.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion will reduce the propensity for grain-boundary fracture.
Reduced grain-boundary fracture will improve toughness after thermal exposure.
The boron-containing alloy will retain greater Charpy impact toughness or other toughness metrics than an otherwise comparable boron-free alloy processed and tested under the same conditions.
The toughness benefit from boron will be most significant above 500°C and less pronounced at lower temperatures.
Solute atoms and grain boundaries can influence the mechanical behavior of crystalline metallic materials.
The optimal boron concentration and the high-entropy-alloy compositions most likely to benefit are unknown.

contradictions.description: The central prediction is that boron must improve toughness relative to the control, so failure to improve toughness would directly refute that prediction. The stated falsification rule, however, requires both no toughness improvement and no detectable boron segregation, meaning that a sample with segregation but no toughness improvement would not be declared falsifying.
